surface_summary: Custer Pennington is arrested and convicted for the murder of Wilson Crumb, a narcotics peddler and actor-director. Shannon Burke, a former addict and friend of the Penningtons, is also charged but later acquitted. The case appears straightforward with circumstantial evidence pointing to Custer, but underlying criminal activities and family secrets complicate the truth.
accepted_facts: Wilson Crumb was found dead with a gunshot wound.
Custer Pennington was found near the crime scene with the victim’s horseshoe.
Shannon Burke had a past association with Crumb and was seen erasing tracks near the body.
Guy Evans was involved in bootlegging stolen whisky and had motive against Crumb.
inferred_conclusions: Custer Pennington was the murderer motivated by jealousy and love.
Shannon Burke was an accomplice or accessory to the murder.
Guy Evans was innocent and uninvolved in the murder.
mechanism_description: Guy Evans killed Wilson Crumb in revenge for Crumb’s role in the downfall and death of his sister Grace. Evans rode to Crumb’s camp, confronted him, and shot him. To divert suspicion, Slick Allen planted evidence implicating Custer Pennington by placing the horse’s missing shoe under the body and misleading authorities. Shannon Burke, unaware of the full truth, initially tried to protect Custer by erasing tracks.
delivery_path: Guy Evans learns of Crumb’s abuse and death of his sister Grace.
Evans obtains a pistol and rides to Crumb’s camp in Jackknife Cañon.
Evans confronts and shoots Crumb during a nighttime encounter.
Evans hides the pistol and rides away to avoid suspicion.
Slick Allen, fearing exposure, plants Custer Pennington’s horseshoe at the crime scene.
Authorities arrest Custer based on circumstantial evidence and planted clues.
Shannon Burke attempts to erase tracks, unknowingly complicating the investigation.
outcome_result: Guy Evans confesses to the murder, exonerating Custer Pennington, who is released before execution.

false_assumption.statement: Custer Pennington was the murderer because he was found near the crime scene with incriminating evidence.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Custer was found with the victim’s horseshoe and had no solid alibi, and circumstantial evidence and witness testimony pointed to him. The prosecution presented a coherent narrative of jealousy and opportunity.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It hides the fact that the real murderer was Guy Evans, who had motive and opportunity, and that the evidence was planted by a third party to frame Custer.

supporting_points: Found near the crime scene with the victim’s horseshoe under the body
Had a pistol matching the murder weapon in his room
Was seen riding near the victim’s camp on the night of the murder
Had a motive of jealousy and love for Shannon Burke
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The evidence was circumstantial and some was planted by a criminal associate to frame him.

red_herrings.description: Shannon Burke was seen sweeping the trail near the murder scene and had a past with the victim.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: She was trying to erase tracks to protect Custer, not to hide her own guilt.

red_herrings.description: Slick Allen’s threats and criminal background suggested he might have committed the murder or framed others.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Allen was involved in narcotics and bootlegging but did not commit the murder; he planted evidence to protect himself.

closed_circle.rationale: The suspects were limited to those with access to the victim and motive: Custer for jealousy, Shannon for association, Guy for revenge, and Allen for criminal self-protection.

discriminating_test.design: Reenact the movements of the horses and riders on the night of the murder, including the timing of the pack train and the location of the murder. Compare the horseshoes and tracks found at the scene with those of the Pennington horses and the burros. Verify the presence or absence of the murder weapon with each suspect.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: This test reveals who had physical access to the crime scene at the time of the murder and whose horseshoes and tracks match those found. It also clarifies who could have carried the murder weapon.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The reenactment confirms that only Guy Evans’s movements and horse tracks align with the murder scene and timing, and that the murder weapon was not in Shannon’s possession.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the characters’ movements, the timing of the pack train, and the physical evidence such as horseshoes and tracks. Shannon’s suspicious behavior and Allen’s threats are presented with plausible innocent explanations. The confession of Guy Evans and the planting of evidence by Allen are foreshadowed through dialogue and character interactions. Careful attention to these clues allows the reader to deduce the true culprit and the framing scheme.
